items.title: What is Node.js, and when is it a good backend choice?
items.answer: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser. It supplies network, file and process APIs (application programming interfaces). V8 executes JavaScript; libuv supports event-loop and operating-system work. Waiting on many database or network calls suits this model. A long calculation still needs a capacity plan. Here Node runs four separate NestJS service processes, selected by SERVICE.

items.title: Does const make an object immutable?
items.answer: No. const prevents assigning a different value to the binding; it does not freeze the referenced object. Catalog can push query parameters into its const values array. Example: const a = []; a.push(1) works, but a = [] fails. Shared nested objects can still change unless copied or deliberately protected.

items.title: What is a closure, and do two requests share its local variables?
items.answer: A closure is a function that keeps access to the scope where it was created. Catalog search creates an add function that remembers that call’s values array. Another search call gets another array. Moving that array to a singleton field would change its lifetime and risk mixing requests. Closures can also retain large objects after they are no longer useful.

items.title: What do destructuring, rest and spread actually copy?
items.answer: Destructuring extracts properties; rest collects the remaining properties. Object spread creates a shallow copy: nested arrays may still point at the same data. Catalog removes ownerEmail before storing the public document, then overrides protected rating fields after spreading an update. The later property wins. This is a data-shaping step, not a substitute for schema and ownership checks.

items.title: How do truthiness, optional chaining and nullish defaults differ?
items.answer: Optional chaining, ?. , stops property access on null or undefined. The ?? operator supplies a default only for those two values; || also replaces 0, false and empty text. Identity uses account?.password_hash ?? this.dummyHash. Catalog tests maxRate !== undefined so zero remains a real filter. The string "false" is truthy and needs an explicit conversion rule.
concepts: Truthiness, optional chaining and nullish defaults

items.title: When should I use map, filter, Set or Map?
items.answer: map transforms array elements; filter selects them. Set keeps distinct values; Map stores key/value pairs without converting every key to text. The comparison hook filters saved input to strings, deduplicates IDs with Set and keeps at most three. Objects in Set compare by identity: two separately created objects with the same fields remain two entries. These collections live in memory, not in a durable database.

items.title: Can a catch block assume the thrown value is an Error?
items.answer: No. JavaScript can throw a string, null or another value. Narrow an unknown caught value before reading its properties. The project filter distinguishes Zod errors, HTTP exceptions and unexpected errors; unexpected details stay in server logs while the client receives a generic message. A surrounding try catches an awaited rejection, but does not automatically catch an unrelated later callback’s throw.

items.title: How do unknown, any and type assertions affect input safety?
items.answer: unknown requires narrowing before use; any turns off useful checking. An assertion such as input as Provider changes the compiler’s opinion without checking a single incoming field. Catalog accepts unknown input and calls providerSchema.parse at runtime. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) from a client or another service still needs validation after a successful TypeScript build.

items.title: What are literal unions and as const useful for?
items.answer: A literal union restricts a type to named alternatives, such as the four service names. as const preserves exact tuple values for deriving that union. These restrictions disappear at runtime: SERVICE arrives as environment text, so serviceName still checks membership. A cast inside includes does not validate the value; the includes result and thrown error perform that check.

items.title: Does a generic return type validate a response?
items.answer: No. Generics express relationships between types. The client api<T> helper tells TypeScript which result callers expect, then parses response JSON. It does not decode the fields against T. Runtime response schemas would be an explicit extension. Compare the backend Catalog lookup, which really parses the returned object with Zod before using ownerEmail.

items.title: Why can Nest inject a class but not an erased interface by itself?
items.answer: A class can supply a runtime constructor value; an interface or object type disappears after compilation. Catalog’s constructor parameter uses Database as the dependency token Nest can resolve. Injecting an interface needs an explicit runtime token and matching provider registration. TypeScript private and readonly describe access and assignment checks; neither creates database permissions or an authorization boundary.

items.title: Why do these TypeScript files import local .js paths?
items.answer: The backend is an ECMAScript module (ESM) package: package.json sets type to module and TypeScript uses NodeNext. Its emitted files run as JavaScript, so ./config.js names the runtime file while TypeScript resolves the source .ts file during compilation. CommonJS uses require/module.exports and has different loading rules. Copying a require tutorial directly into this ESM package can fail at startup.

items.title: Why can decorator settings break dependency injection?
items.answer: This Nest setup uses decorator metadata emitted by TypeScript and loads reflect-metadata before bootstrap. The emitted constructor information helps resolve class dependencies. experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata are part of that compiler/runtime agreement. Changing decorator mode requires checking compatibility. Declaration packages such as @types/pg add compile-time descriptions; installing them does not install pg’s runtime code or validate database results.

items.title: Does await block every request or start a new thread?
items.answer: Neither. await suspends the current async function’s continuation until its promise settles, allowing other callbacks to run while external work waits. Identity can await PostgreSQL while another request progresses. Promises and async/await do not themselves execute JavaScript on extra processors. Two requests can interleave across awaits, so one main JavaScript thread does not remove database races.

items.title: How do callbacks, promises and async/await relate?
items.answer: A callback is a function another operation invokes. A promise represents a future result or rejection; async functions return promises and await consumes them. Password code uses promisify to adapt Node’s error-first scrypt callback, whose first argument reports failure. The wrapper keeps scrypt asynchronous; it does not create a new password algorithm. Callbacks remain appropriate for repeated events, while a promise settles once.

items.title: How is the native worker pool different from worker_threads?
items.answer: Asynchronous scrypt uses native worker-pool capacity, so the main event loop can serve other work. Heavy JavaScript still occupies its current thread, even inside an async function. worker_threads can run JavaScript in parallel on other threads; this application has no worker-thread job pool. Both designs consume finite processor and memory capacity, so unlimited parallel password work remains unsafe.

items.title: Does Promise.all limit concurrency or cancel failed work?
items.answer: No. map starts each provider lookup; Promise.all aggregates the returned promises in input order and rejects when one rejects. Already started operations continue unless separately cancelled. The project caps comparisons at three, bounding that particular fan-out. For a large batch, queue work with a measured concurrency limit. Use allSettled when every success/failure outcome is needed, not when partial success should silently count as a complete result.
concepts: Promise aggregation is not a concurrency limiter

items.title: Are timers exact, and what does unref change?
items.answer: A timeout makes its callback eligible after a delay; busy JavaScript can postpone it. unref means that timer alone need not keep the process alive. It neither cancels the callback nor stops network work. The outbox worker uses an unreferenced pause for polling. A ref-count decision is about process lifetime, not a guarantee that a final retry or cleanup will execute.

items.title: What order do promises, nextTick, setTimeout and setImmediate run in?
items.answer: Synchronous code finishes first; queued promise continuations run before the next timer turn. process.nextTick has a separate queue and recursive use can starve input/output (I/O). Do not promise one universal nextTick-versus-promise order across CommonJS and ESM entry points. Nor is top-level setTimeout(0) versus setImmediate order guaranteed. In an I/O callback, immediate runs before a timer scheduled there. State the execution context before predicting output.

items.title: Why is void backgroundWork() not an error handler?
items.answer: void discards an expression’s value; it does not catch promise rejection. The messaging bootstrap launches an ongoing loop with void this.run(); the loop owns retries, health status and cleanup. Awaiting that never-ending loop during bootstrap would prevent startup completing. Detached work needs a deliberate error owner and stop policy; merely prefixing an unsafe promise with void does not supply either.
concepts: Detached promises need their own error policy

items.title: What does backpressure mean beyond streams?
items.answer: Backpressure means slowing or limiting incoming work when a dependency cannot keep up. The database pool allows ten connections per process; additional work waits, with a five-second acquisition limit. That bounds connections, not all queued requests or query execution time. Measure waiting work and downstream latency before raising limits; four services and multiple replicas multiply the total connection budget.

items.title: Is EventEmitter.emit asynchronous?
items.answer: By default, emit calls registered listeners synchronously in registration order. A listener can schedule later work, but emit does not await a promise it returns. A plain EventEmitter error event without an error listener can terminate the process. Database registers a pool error listener for failures from idle clients. Local event listeners are not durable Kafka delivery and cannot replace the persisted outbox.

items.title: What does HTTP body parsing prove, and what does it not prove?
items.answer: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) carries a method, path, headers and body bytes. Express’s JSON parser turns permitted input into a JavaScript value, subject to a 128-kilobyte limit. Valid JSON can still have the wrong fields, role or owner, so schema and business checks follow. Malformed syntax, excessive size and a rejected domain request fail at different boundaries; returning the same status does not make those causes identical.

items.title: Why is string length different from Buffer byte length?
items.answer: JavaScript string length counts UTF-16 code units; Buffer represents bytes. UTF-8 (Unicode Transformation Format, 8-bit) uses variable-width encoding: an emoji such as 😀 has string length 2 and byte length 4. The JSON Web Token secret (JWT_SECRET) is checked in bytes, while INTERNAL_API_KEY is checked in characters. Hex decoding in password verification and UTF-8 decoding in Kafka serve different purposes; choose the encoding explicitly.

items.title: When are readFile and readdir appropriate?
items.answer: readFile reads an entire file before resolving; readdir lists directory entries. That is reasonable for the small, trusted SQL (Structured Query Language) migration files loaded at startup. The migration runner filters service-prefixed numbered filenames and sorts them. A multi-gigabyte upload would need incremental processing and size limits instead. Async file reads avoid blocking the main loop on disk waits but still require memory for the returned contents.

items.title: How does process.cwd differ from the current module location?
items.answer: process.cwd() is the process’s working directory, which launchers can choose. import.meta.url identifies the current ESM module. Database locates migrations relative to cwd, so running node backend/dist/main.js from the repository root can look in the wrong migrations directory. Use the supplied backend start scripts and working directory. If deliberately redesigning paths, anchor them to a module URL and test the packaged layout.

items.title: What is a stream, and why use pipeline for large data?
items.answer: A stream processes chunks instead of first building the whole result in memory. Readable produces chunks, Writable consumes them, Duplex does both, and Transform changes chunks. pipeline connects stages and propagates completion or errors. This app has no streaming-upload endpoint; its small migration-file read is only the contrast. A practice stream copy should prove identical destination bytes and exercise an error case.

items.title: What should a producer do when writable.write returns false?
items.answer: Pause production until the writable signals drain; false means the chunk was accepted but the internal buffer reached its threshold. Ignoring it keeps buffering and can exhaust memory. highWaterMark is a buffering threshold, not a universal memory ceiling. pipeline handles normal stream backpressure for you. The current application does not implement a custom stream producer; database pool limits teach a related resource-budget idea.

items.title: How are child processes, watch mode and compiled output related?
items.answer: spawn starts another operating-system process with its own memory and lifecycle. The backend developer launcher first compiles TypeScript, then runs a compiler watcher and Node’s watcher over emitted JavaScript. Saving source is not the same as successfully compiling or passing tests. By default a child inherits process.env. Supplying env replaces that environment unless the parent spreads its values into the new object. Ordinary JavaScript variables are not shared between processes.

items.title: Why choose spawn or execFile over a shell command string?
items.answer: exec runs through a shell; untrusted metacharacters can become commands. spawn/execFile with a fixed executable, argument array and shell disabled avoid shell interpretation. They still need input rules because the called program can interpret dangerous options or paths. The backend launcher selects from four known service names and invokes process.execPath directly. Shell escaping is not replaced by JSON.stringify.

items.title: What should SIGTERM and shutdown hooks accomplish?
items.answer: SIGTERM asks a process to stop; Nest shutdown hooks let providers close resources. Database ends its pool and messaging workers disconnect. Normal shutdown should stop new work and allow bounded in-flight work to finish, but forced termination can bypass hooks. That is why durable transactions, outbox replay and consumer deduplication remain necessary. process.exitCode marks the eventual status without immediately terminating pending work.

items.title: When would worker threads or cluster help, and are they implemented here?
items.answer: Worker threads can run processor-heavy JavaScript in parallel and communicate through messages. Cluster starts separate Node processes that can share a listening port. Neither makes database transactions magically consistent, and cluster workers do not share ordinary in-memory state. The project runs one process per capability; it implements neither a worker-thread job pool nor Node cluster. Container replicas are another process-scaling choice.

items.answer: AsyncLocalStorage can carry request-scoped data through supported asynchronous continuations without a mutable global currentRequest variable. That helps correlate logs while concurrent requests interleave. It does not authenticate a caller or persist an audit trail. The project’s current ErrorFilter logs errors without an AsyncLocalStorage request context; request-context middleware would be an explicit extension.

items.title: Does fetch reject an HTTP error response, and what does abort guarantee?
items.answer: fetch rejects for transport failure or an aborted operation, but a received HTTP 404 or 500 still needs an explicit status check. Inquiries checks response.status and response.ok and bounds Catalog lookup with AbortSignal.timeout(5000). Abort limits client waiting; it does not undo work the remote server may already have committed. Retry writes with their original idempotency key when the outcome is uncertain.

items.title: How would you investigate memory growth without assuming a leak?
items.answer: Compare heap, external Buffer memory and whole-process memory under a repeatable workload. Live caches, retained closures, unfinished requests and excessive buffering can all grow usage. A garbage-collected language can still retain reachable objects forever. This project has no built-in heap-capture workflow; use controlled local diagnostic runs and treat snapshots as sensitive because they may contain tokens or request data.

items.title: What do JSON.parse and JSON.stringify preserve?
items.answer: JSON.parse decodes JSON syntax; it does not establish the expected object shape. JSON.stringify creates JSON text and can fail on circular references or BigInt values. Object properties with undefined are omitted, and a Date normally serializes through its ISO text representation. The catalog seed path parses trusted file contents, then validates each public document. Avoid using JSON round-trips as a universal deep-clone or input-validation technique.

items.title: How should a backend use regular expressions and number conversion?
items.answer: A regular expression checks a text pattern, not business permission. The migration regex accepts numbered SQL (Structured Query Language) filenames after the service-prefix check; neither permits user-chosen arbitrary file paths. PORT is converted with Number and checked for integer range before listening. Number("") becomes zero and parseInt can accept a valid prefix followed by junk, so validate the whole external value. Avoid unbounded complex regexes on large untrusted input.

items.title: Why serialize timestamps with toISOString?
items.answer: A Date represents a time value, while toISOString emits a standardized UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) timestamp ending in Z. Inquiries converts the stored creation timestamp before returning it. Local display time can differ by time zone. Validate external date input deliberately; an invalid Date makes toISOString throw. Use durations and monotonic clocks for elapsed-time measurement rather than assuming wall-clock dates never jump.

items.title: When should I use URL, URLSearchParams and encodeURIComponent?
items.answer: URL parses an address into named components; it does not by itself approve a host or protocol. Config separately permits only HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) or HTTPS (HTTP over Transport Layer Security) for Catalog. URLSearchParams encodes query names and values. encodeURIComponent protects a single path component, such as a provider ID; do not encode the entire URL as though it were one ID. The server must still validate decoded input and authorization.

These helpers avoid duplicated type declarations, but never remove a sensitive property from a real object or check an incoming payload.

items.answer: import type tells TypeScript an import is needed only for checking types; it disappears from emitted JavaScript. The HTTP helper imports Auth this way because Auth is a type description. A class used by Nest dependency injection must remain available as a runtime value/token. items.title: Why do launchers use fileURLToPath, dirname, resolve and process groups?
items.answer: An ECMAScript module (ESM) URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is not automatically an operating-system file path. fileURLToPath converts it safely, dirname gets its containing directory and resolve forms an absolute project path. The root developer launcher uses that anchor even when invoked elsewhere. On Unix it starts detached process groups and sends SIGTERM to the group, so nested compiler/server children can stop together; Windows has a different child-kill path.

items.title: How do arrow functions and class methods use this?
items.answer: An arrow captures this from its surrounding scope; it does not get a new receiver when called as another object’s property. A normal method uses its call receiver, so passing an unbound method can lose the intended instance. Nest creates class instances and injects their constructor dependencies. Catalog’s local add arrow closes over per-call query values; moving request data onto a singleton field would change its sharing and lifetime.

items.checks: Read the failed path and process working directory. Database joins process.cwd() with migrations; Catalog/Identity also read seeds relative to cwd. Check packaged migrations and seeds exist and match the selected SERVICE. Do not print .env or database credentials while diagnosing.

items.title: The service hangs on shutdown or restarts mid-delivery

items.checks: Inspect shutdown hooks, pool.end, worker stopping flags and disconnect calls. Check open sockets/timers and whether an external call can wait indefinitely. Determine whether an event was acknowledged before its database bookkeeping; repeated delivery can be a legitimate crash window.

Verify the service becomes healthy and pending events complete with one durable notification per event identity. Also test a forced termination, because graceful shutdown alone does not cover crashes.

items.title: What do Nest decorators and modules do?
items.answer: Decorators attach information to classes and methods; Nest reads it to find routes and providers. The module registers which objects belong in this application. Here SERVICE selects one capability before Nest starts. Importing a class alone does not register it, and @Injectable does not itself open a database connection.

items.title: How does dependency injection supply a service?
items.answer: Dependency injection means Nest supplies required objects through a constructor. Database is registered as a provider, so CatalogService receives it. The default instance is shared inside one application context; another process has another instance. Interfaces disappear after compilation, so an interface needs a runtime injection token. private readonly stores the argument and prevents rebinding; the referenced pool remains mutable.

items.title: What belongs in a controller versus a service?
items.answer: A controller translates a Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) request into a service call: it reads route parameters, headers and input. A service performs the business decision and database work. Catalog declares /me before /:id so the named route is not swallowed by a dynamic identifier. Keep ownership checks in the execution path even if the page already hides a button.

items.title: When is asynchronous startup finished?
items.answer: Nest can await a Promise returned from an initialization hook. Database migrations complete in onModuleInit; Identity awaits a dummy password hash in onApplicationBootstrap. A detached background loop such as void this.run() does not delay startup until Kafka connects. Do not assume unrelated providers initialize in their array order; express required dependencies explicitly.

items.title: Are Helmet, body parsing and validation interchangeable?
items.answer: No. Helmet adds security response headers. The JSON parser turns request bytes into a JavaScript value and rejects bodies beyond 128kb. Zod checks the resulting fields. JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) that parses successfully can still contain an invalid budget or unexpected fields. Here parsing is configured explicitly with Nest bodyParser disabled to avoid competing parser limits.

items.title: How do guards and exception filters differ?
items.answer: A guard allows or rejects entry to a route; AuthGuard verifies a token and attaches the actor. A filter turns thrown failures into HTTP responses. ErrorFilter maps schema failures to 400, preserves known HTTP statuses and hides unexpected 500 details. Passing a guard establishes an identity; the service must still check ownership of the requested row.

items.title: Does installing RxJS make these services reactive?
items.answer: RxJS, Reactive Extensions for JavaScript, offers Observables: subscriptions can receive multiple values and can be cancelled. This backend installs RxJS for Nest but its application services use Promises and KafkaJS callbacks. It has no custom Observable pipeline. Describe the mechanism actually present before proposing reactive operators.
items.worked_example: In an isolated RxJS example, subscribe to the documented Observable that emits 1, 2 and 3 synchronously, then 4 after a delay and completes. Record the values in order and unsubscribe from a continuing source to stop future emissions. This is an extension, not a marketplace pipeline.
items.lesson_relation: Lesson05 teaches that RxJS is installed without custom application Observable pipelines. The external subscription example is a worked extension, not an implemented marketplace feature.

items.title: Why validate input when TypeScript already has types?
items.answer: TypeScript checks code before it runs; incoming requests have no trustworthy TypeScript type. Zod parse validates an unknown value at runtime, returns the accepted value or throws. Here an invalid inquiry budget becomes 400 before persistence. A type assertion such as body as CreateInquiry only tells the compiler to trust you; it does not inspect the request.

items.title: How do coercion, transforms and defaults affect query parameters?
items.answer: Query parameters arrive as text. Catalog converts maxRate to a bounded integer, transforms only the strings true and false into booleans, and defaults a missing sort to recommended. Boolean("false") is true because nonempty text is truthy, so arbitrary Boolean coercion would be wrong. Check undefined explicitly so a supplied zero or false is not discarded.

source.excerpt:
available: z
      .enum(['true', 'false'])
      .transform((v) => v === 'true')
      .optional(),
    sort: z.enum(['recommended', 'rate-asc', 'rating']).default('recommended'),

items.title: What do strict schemas and inferred types guarantee?
items.answer: A strict object schema rejects unknown keys; each field separately decides whether it is required, optional or defaulted. Nested objects need their own strictness. z.infer derives a compile-time type from the schema but does not run validation. A valid Provider object still needs an ownership check before an update.

items.title: How are SQL injection and wildcard surprises prevented?
items.answer: Structured Query Language (SQL) values travel separately from query text as $1, $2 and later parameters. Catalog’s add closure captures the values array and supplies the next position. Parameters cannot stand for column names or sort expressions; use fixed allowlisted branches. Escape percent and underscore separately when search should treat them literally: parameters alone do not remove LIKE wildcard meaning.
concepts: Escaping LIKE patterns versus SQL parameters

items.title: How does PostgreSQL JSONB differ from a JavaScript object?
items.answer: JSONB is PostgreSQL’s binary JSON storage, queried inside the database. The -> operator returns JSON and ->> extracts text. Catalog casts hourlyRate text to numeric before comparison and sorting; text ordering would put 100 before 20. An array predicate uses jsonb_array_elements_text for skills. Validate stored documents and consider measured indexes when the dataset grows.

items.title: How does this catalog paginate consistently?
items.answer: The schema bounds page and size; SQL applies LIMIT and OFFSET after a deterministic sort with id as a tie breaker. A common table expression filters once for both total and page items. It can return an empty items array and a nonzero total for an out-of-range page. Large offsets still scan work; cursor pagination is a design extension, not implemented here.

items.title: Why preserve server-owned fields during a profile update?
items.answer: A client must not award itself a rating. Catalog locks the owner’s row, checks that the submitted profile ID matches, then puts stored rating, reviewCount and completedProjects after the submitted fields. Later object properties override earlier ones. This preserves protected values while accepting validated edits; neither schema validity nor a lock alone supplies that business policy.

items.title: What is a connection pool, and how big is this one?
items.answer: A pool reuses database sessions rather than establishing one for every query. This pool allows ten connections per process and waits up to five seconds for connection acquisition. Four service processes can use forty, before extra replicas or operations. Raising max can move overload into PostgreSQL; first measure active, idle and waiting work and shorten slow transactions.

items.title: Why must a transaction keep the same database client?
items.answer: BEGIN, statements and COMMIT must run on one checked-out client because a transaction belongs to that database session. Separate pool.query calls can use different sessions. The wrapper rolls back on failure and releases the client in finally on every path. Releasing without rollback can leave a bad transaction for the next borrower; forgetting release can exhaust the pool.
concepts: try, catch and finally protect resources

items.title: Are database row types automatically the API types?
items.answer: No. A database numeric value may arrive as text, and timestamps may arrive as Date objects. inquiryView deliberately converts budget with Number and createdAt to an International Organization for Standardization (ISO) timestamp string. For larger financial precision, use an exact decimal or minor-unit contract rather than assuming every SQL number fits a JavaScript Number. A generic row annotation alone validates nothing.

source.excerpt:
message: row.message,
    budget: Number(row.budget),
    clientType: row.client_type,
    status: row.status,
    createdAt: new Date(row.created_at).toISOString(),

items.title: When should a row lock or an advisory lock be used?
items.answer: A row lock protects an existing row during a transaction; Catalog uses FOR UPDATE while editing an owned profile. An advisory lock protects an application-defined decision, even before the inquiry row exists. Inquiries hashes the client/key pair into a transaction-scoped lock shared across replicas. Keep database unique constraints too; they enforce the invariant even if another write path omits the lock.

items.title: Does a transaction imply serializable isolation?
items.answer: No. PostgreSQL normally uses Read Committed unless configured otherwise; this wrapper issues BEGIN without selecting a stronger level. Each statement can see a newer committed snapshot. Explicit locks and constraints protect specific decisions here. Serializable transactions can reject conflicting work and require retrying the entire transaction; they are not a free switch that removes every application policy.
items.lesson_relation: Lessons07/16 provide transaction and concurrency prerequisites. The explicit isolation-level comparison is a researched extension supported by PostgreSQL documentation.

items.title: Why are migrations versioned, hashed and locked?
items.answer: A migration changes a database schema in a repeatable sequence. Startup reads only this service’s numbered SQL files, sorts them and records a Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) checksum. An advisory lock prevents two replicas applying the same sequence together. A changed applied file is rejected: add a new migration. Backups and compatible rollout still matter; a checksum cannot recover lost data.

items.title: What do pool error events and verified TLS protect?
items.answer: Idle database clients can fail outside an awaited query, so the pool also has an error listener. Transport Layer Security (TLS) encrypts the connection and verifies its peer. This configuration retains rejectUnauthorized: true and accepts a certificate authority (CA) chain. Do not repair a certificate error by disabling verification. Connection-string ssl settings can replace explicit pg settings; the project rejects that mixture.

items.title: How does promisify connect callbacks to async/await?
items.answer: Node’s scrypt callback follows the error-first convention: an error argument precedes the result. util.promisify wraps that convention in a Promise-returning function, so await can receive the derived bytes and a rejection can be caught. It does not move arbitrary JavaScript work to another thread. Methods that rely on this may also need binding before conversion.

items.title: Why use a salt and scrypt for passwords?
items.answer: scrypt deliberately costs memory and computation; a fast general hash is unsuitable for passwords. A random salt prevents equal passwords from sharing an encoded result and is stored beside the hash. Here 16 random bytes become 32 hexadecimal characters. Async hashing still consumes finite worker capacity, so limit login load and review work factors against current security guidance rather than calling library defaults production hardening.

items.title: Does timingSafeEqual make the whole login constant-time?
items.answer: No. It avoids content-dependent early exit in that equal-length byte comparison. This verifier checks the stored encoding and derives a candidate Buffer first; the rest of login has other timing behavior. A dummy derivation also runs for a missing account to reduce obvious differences, followed by an explicit account-exists check. It cannot authenticate a missing user and does not prove complete timing resistance.
concepts: Optional chaining and a dummy derivation

items.title: What does this JWT prove, and what stays readable?
items.answer: A JSON Web Token (JWT) carries readable encoded claims and a signature, not encrypted private data. This token expires in one hour. HS256 means Hash-based Message Authentication Code with SHA-256: signers and verifiers share a secret. Any verifier possessing it can also mint tokens, so separate asymmetric identity issuance is a production extension. Never put secrets in its payload.

source.excerpt:
return jwt.sign(actor, required('JWT_SECRET'), {
    algorithm: 'HS256',
    issuer: 'marketplace',
    audience: 'marketplace',
    subject: actor.email,

concepts: JWT signing: claims, encoding and HMAC

items.title: Why verify JWT claims as well as its signature?
items.answer: A valid signature alone does not mean the token was intended for this API. verifyActor allowlists HS256 and checks issuer, audience, expiry and the expected principal fields; its subject must equal email. Decoding alone is not verification. Invalid or expired credentials produce 401. A verified actor can still receive 403 when its role or ownership does not allow the requested action.

items.title: How do authentication, roles and ownership differ?
items.answer: Authentication establishes who called; a role narrows which class of action they may attempt. Ownership decides whether they may act on this particular record. Here only the target provider may resolve an inquiry and only the notification recipient may mark it read. Read queries also filter by the actor. A browser-supplied email or a hidden button is not an authorization control.

items.title: What does the in-memory login throttle actually limit?
items.answer: A Map stores counts and expiry per request IP address, with a limit of thirty attempts per minute in each process. Mutating a retrieved object changes that stored object; expired entries are removed on later requests. Another replica has another Map, and restart clears it. This is not a shared distributed limit. Proxy trust and a bounded shared store need deliberate design before public exposure.

items.title: Why handle fetch rejection and response status separately?
items.answer: fetch rejects for network or abort failures, but an HTTP 404 is normally a resolved Response. The provider lookup therefore catches transport errors, handles 404, checks response.ok, then parses JSON and validates its shape. A successful status with malformed data is still a failed dependency contract. The caller receives a controlled error, not a partly trusted owner record.
concepts: Native fetch and two failure channels

items.title: What do a fetch timeout and URL encoding guarantee?
items.answer: AbortSignal.timeout bounds this lookup to five seconds; encodeURIComponent keeps the provider ID inside one path component. Neither supplies an end-to-end request deadline or authorization. The lookup uses a distinct internal service key, not a browser JWT. Its database transaction and advisory lock remain occupied during the lookup, so slow dependencies can consume pool capacity.
concepts: A timeout is one bounded wait

items.title: How does an idempotency key differ from a payload fingerprint?
items.answer: The key names one logical submission and is scoped to the authenticated client. The fingerprint hashes a fixed-order array of validated fields to detect changed content. Reusing the same key and content returns the original inquiry; changed content yields 409. Generate and preserve the key before sending. A timeout is uncertain outcome, so retry the original key and payload rather than creating a second submission.

items.title: Why generate separate inquiry and event UUIDs?
items.answer: A Universally Unique Identifier (UUID) labels one record; randomUUID generates one without a central counter. The inquiry ID identifies the business request, while the event ID identifies the notification-producing occurrence. Neither replaces the client’s retry key. Keeping these identities separate lets a durable event replay retain its identity and allows future events about the same inquiry.

items.title: How does an outbox avoid losing an event intent?
items.answer: The inquiry row and outbox row commit in one PostgreSQL transaction. Either both exist or neither does. A later publisher sends the persisted event, waits for Kafka acknowledgment and marks it published. An HTTP success proves a durable inquiry and event intent; it does not prove inbox delivery. No transaction here atomically covers both Kafka and PostgreSQL, so consumer deduplication is required.
concepts: Outbox: one database transaction, two records

items.title: What makes inquiry status transitions safe?
items.answer: The inquiry row is locked while the service checks ownership and current status. PENDING may become ACCEPTED or DECLINED. Repeating the same final decision returns that state; trying the other decision after resolution yields 409. Database checks restrict stored status values, and the unique client/key constraint protects submission identity. A valid enum alone cannot enforce ownership or transition order.

items.title: What are Kafka’s client, producer, consumer and group?
items.answer: KafkaJS connects Node to a broker. A producer sends topic records; a consumer reads assigned partitions. clientId labels an application for diagnostics, whereas groupId identifies consumers sharing partition work and resume positions. Notifications uses one stable group. Starting another group reads independently and can reproduce effects unless the destination still deduplicates event identities.

items.title: Do keys and acks=-1 guarantee exactly-once processing?
items.answer: No. The inquiry ID key helps route related records to a partition, where offsets give order. acks=-1 waits for the in-sync replicas required by the broker configuration; a one-broker setup still has one copy. A publisher can crash after acknowledgment but before marking the outbox row. Its retry may resend the same event. There is no global order across partitions.

items.title: Why publish a bounded SKIP LOCKED batch?
items.answer: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets competing publishers take unlocked outbox rows without waiting on each other. LIMIT 25 bounds each transaction’s batch; it does not bound the entire backlog. Publishing happens while row locks and the database client are held, so broker delays lengthen transactions. Multiple publishers may deliver batches out of creation order; strict ordering would need an additional design.

items.title: Does fromBeginning replay every record on every restart?
items.answer: No. A consumer group normally resumes at its committed offset, which is its saved position per partition. fromBeginning: true chooses the earliest available position only when no valid committed position exists. Retention may already have removed older records. Rebalancing redistributes partitions as members join or fail; it can cause replay around unfinished work.

items.title: Why decode, parse and validate an event separately?
items.answer: Kafka transports bytes. Buffer.toString decodes UTF-8, an encoding of text into bytes; JSON.parse then creates a JavaScript value. Zod finally checks its required fields and types. Valid JSON can still be an invalid event. The consumer awaits durable notification insertion before its handler succeeds; failures must not be treated as successfully processed records.

items.title: How can repeated event delivery produce one inbox row?
items.answer: Notifications stores a unique event_id and uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. The receipt identity and inbox effect are the same database write. A crash after insertion but before offset commit may replay the event; that insertion becomes a no-op. This is an idempotent effect with at-least-once transport, not proof that the event was transported exactly once.

await this.db.query(
      'INSERT INTO notifications(id,event_id,inquiry_id,recipient_email,message,created_at) VALUES($1,$2,$3,$4,$5,$6) ON CONFLICT(event_id) DO NOTHING',
      [
        randomUUID(),
        event.eventId,

concepts: Unique event IDs make duplicate effects harmless

items.title: Why can HTTP start while the messaging worker reconnects?
items.answer: The bootstrap hook starts a background Promise without awaiting the whole loop. Startup connection failures are caught and retried; consumer failures after run starts follow KafkaJS’s separate crash/restart policy and can leave a stopped worker. The pause uses an unreferenced timer, which alone will not keep Node alive. void does not catch rejections. Graceful completion and shutdown races still need tests.

items.title: What do KafkaJS instrumentation events say about health?
items.answer: The consumer updates a local flag on group join, crash and disconnect. KafkaJS instrumentation listeners run asynchronously, which differs from ordinary synchronous Node EventEmitter listeners. A group join proves membership at that point, not a caught-up inbox or successful business processing. Observe lag and processing errors too; a flag may lag a failure or remain true while a poison record blocks progress. Inspect the CRASH restart flag and actual offset/insert progress: a stopped consumer can leave this application’s outer loop sleeping.

items.title: Why expose three different health checks?
items.answer: Liveness reports a responding process. Serving health queries the database and permits durable inquiry writes while messaging retries. Readiness also checks the messaging worker flag where applicable. Neither a green probe nor nginx’s static /health proves a login-to-inquiry-to-notification journey. Restarting a live process for every dependency failure can turn one outage into a restart storm.

items.title: Does a shared backend image mean one service or one failure domain?
items.answer: One build contains the code, but SERVICE selects one controller, provider set and service-owned database per process. There are four capability boundaries. Their shared PostgreSQL host can still fail all four locally; an image or shared library defect can affect them together. Independent processes enable separate scaling but do not automatically create high availability or independent data ownership.
concepts: Shared build versus independent failure domains

items.title: Does FOR UPDATE prevent a stale profile overwrite?
items.answer: It serializes database writers while the transaction runs. It does not know that a user opened an older profile in a second tab. Catalog has no profile version or entity tag comparison, so two accepted full updates can overwrite editable fields. Optimistic concurrency would compare a version and reject a stale update so the user can reload and merge.
items.worked_example: Practice with a separate conditional-update server: GET version 7 with its entity tag, send an update with If-Match for version 7 and advance to 8; repeat the old condition and expect 412 Precondition Failed. Persist and compare the version atomically. The marketplace does not currently expose this contract.
items.lesson_relation: Lesson16 teaches the row-lock versus stale-user conflict distinction and labels optimistic version checking absent. The If-Match worked example is an external extension.

items.title: How do CORS and CSRF differ from login protection?
items.answer: Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) controls browser access across origins; it is not an authorization boundary for arbitrary clients. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) abuses credentials a browser attaches automatically, especially cookies. This app uses same-origin proxies and explicit bearer headers; it does not implement a cookie-session CSRF flow. If that design changes, add explicit origin and CSRF controls rather than treating Helmet as a substitute.
items.worked_example: In a separate Nest app, enable CORS for one explicit test origin and PUT, with Authorization allowed. Send an OPTIONS preflight from that origin and inspect the allowed-origin/method headers; repeat from another origin and verify no readable cross-origin response. Then test server authorization directly because CORS does not stop non-browser callers.
items.lesson_relation: Lessons08/16 are security and reliability prerequisites; they do not teach CORS or CSRF. This is a researched extension taught by the linked official documentation and external worked example.

items.title: How do sessions, OAuth and OpenID Connect differ from this JWT login?
items.answer: A server session normally stores login state server-side and sends a session identifier cookie. OAuth 2.0 delegates access; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer. This project implements neither federation nor refresh/session revocation: it issues its own one-hour bearer token. A logged-out browser can discard it, but an already copied valid token stays usable until expiry unless server-side revocation is added.
items.worked_example: Use Appendix B’s Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) test vector in a separate local script: SHA-256 hash the published verifier, then base64url encode the bytes. Expect challenge E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM. In an authorization-code flow, bind that challenge at authorization and require the original verifier at code exchange. This demonstrates code binding, not a deployed identity provider.
items.lesson_relation: Lesson08 provides JWT authentication prerequisites; it does not teach sessions, OAuth, OpenID Connect or PKCE. These are researched extensions taught by the linked official specifications and external worked example.

items.title: What does graceful shutdown promise here?
items.answer: Nest shutdown hooks are enabled, database destruction ends its pool, and messaging destruction sets stopping and disconnects the client. A shutdown signal is not a guarantee that every in-flight request or detached loop drained before termination. The process needs time to finish; a forced kill skips hooks. Test shutdown under active work and verify durable retries instead of assuming every hook establishes lossless delivery.

items.title: What should application logs prove without leaking secrets?
items.answer: Logs should identify the failing operation and enough safe context to connect it with a request or event. ErrorFilter hides unexpected server details from clients while logging the error internally; worker logs name retry failures. Do not log bearer tokens, passwords or connection strings. Structured correlation across requests and events is an extension; the existing logger alone is not a distributed trace.
items.lesson_relation: Lessons16/17 provide reliability and delivery prerequisites. Safe correlation-log design is a researched extension; current ErrorFilter output is the project example.

items.title: In which order do middleware, guards, pipes and interceptors run?
items.answer: On the usual successful path, middleware runs first, then guards, interceptor entry, pipes and the controller/service; interceptor response handling unwinds in reverse order. Filters handle uncaught failures rather than a mandatory success stage. Middleware handles requests broadly, a guard decides access, a pipe validates/transforms arguments and an interceptor wraps execution. This project uses middleware, AuthGuard and ErrorFilter; it calls Zod directly and has no custom application pipe/interceptor.
items.worked_example: In the official ParseIntPipe route example, bind ParseIntPipe to an id parameter. Request /cats/42 and inspect a number passed to the handler; request /cats/nope and expect 400 before the handler. Add a logging interceptor in an isolated app to observe its before/after execution around that handler. These are practice additions, not current marketplace registrations.
items.lesson_relation: Lessons05/19 provide Nest wiring and source-inventory prerequisites. Full middleware/guard/pipe/interceptor ordering is a researched extension; custom application pipes and interceptors are absent.

items.title: Does this project use ConfigModule?
items.answer: No. validateConfig and required read process.env directly and fail startup for missing or invalid settings. Nest ConfigModule is an optional configuration package, not automatically installed by using Nest. Both approaches still need runtime checks, separate environment values and secret handling. Never print a whole environment object while troubleshooting.
items.worked_example: In a separate Nest example, register ConfigModule.forRoot with a validation function that rejects a nonnumeric PORT. Start with PORT=abc and expect startup rejection; use a valid port and read the validated value through ConfigService. Do not assume this marketplace has ConfigService injection or automatic .env loading.
items.lesson_relation: Lessons05/19 provide Nest wiring and source-inventory prerequisites. ConfigModule usage is a researched extension and is absent from this project.

items.title: Is pg an object-relational mapper?
items.answer: No. pg sends SQL and returns rows; this project explicitly writes queries, transactions and migrations. An object-relational mapper (ORM) maps entities to database operations; TypeORM and Prisma are absent. An ORM can reduce mapping code but does not remove query planning, ownership checks or transaction boundaries. Do not invent repositories or entity decorators when explaining this source.
items.worked_example: In the separate official TypeORM example, define a User entity, register TypeOrmModule.forFeature([User]) and inject its Repository into UsersService. Insert a synthetic user, find it, restart and read it again from the configured database. Examine generated SQL and ensure the database is isolated; none of these entity/repository registrations exists here.
items.lesson_relation: Lessons07/19 teach the actual pg/SQL approach and source inventory. The TypeORM repository example is a researched external extension; an ORM is absent here.

items.title: Does AuthGuard here use Passport strategies?
items.answer: No. It is the project’s own Nest guard calling jsonwebtoken directly. Passport is an authentication integration with strategies such as local credentials or bearer-token validation; its Nest module is absent. Switching adapters would still require verified claims and resource ownership checks, and would not create external identity federation by itself.
items.worked_example: Follow the external local-strategy example in an isolated Nest app: implement validate(username,password), register the strategy and use AuthGuard("local") on a test login route. A valid synthetic user reaches the handler as request.user; a wrong password yields 401. Keep marketplace JWT and ownership behavior intact if evaluating a migration.
items.lesson_relation: Lessons08/19 provide actual JWT-guard and source-inventory prerequisites. Passport strategies are a researched external extension and are absent here.

items.title: Are these API schemas generated by Swagger?
items.answer: No. CONTRACT.md documents the interface and Zod enforces input; there is no Swagger/OpenAPI module or generated specification in this app. OpenAPI is a machine-readable API description and Swagger tooling can render it. Documentation generation and runtime validation are separate; a page of schemas does not prove actual route behavior matches.
items.worked_example: In the external Nest Swagger bootstrap example, build a document using DocumentBuilder and SwaggerModule.createDocument, then mount it with SwaggerModule.setup. Inspect the resulting paths and try a synthetic endpoint. Verify 400/401/error responses separately against real requests; this marketplace does not expose that generated document.
items.lesson_relation: Lessons06/19 provide runtime-schema and source-inventory prerequisites. Generated Swagger/OpenAPI documentation is a researched external extension and is absent here.

items.title: Login returns 401 even with a token: where do you look?
items.answer: Separate a missing or invalid credential from a permission failure. Use a synthetic test account, never print its bearer token in evidence.

source.symbol: throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid or expired bearer token');

items.symptom: Authenticated requests return 401 after login or between services.
items.checks: Check the Authorization Bearer header, expiry, clock, issuer/audience, allowlisted algorithm and that service secret configuration belongs to the same environment; inspect names/presence without exposing values.
items.repair: Restore the intended environment configuration or log in again for an expired token. Keep verification and claim checks enabled.
items.recovery: A fresh valid token returns /api/auth/me; an expired or tampered token remains 401, and another owner still cannot edit protected data.

items.title: Catalog returns 400 or an unexpected search page: how do you diagnose it?
items.answer: Distinguish schema rejection from query behavior; changing validation just to make a request pass can break the API contract.

source.excerpt:
available: z
      .enum(['true', 'false'])
      .transform((v) => v === 'true')
      .optional(),
    sort: z.enum(['recommended', 'rate-asc', 'rating']).default('recommended'),

items.symptom: A search returns 400, false behaves like true, or rate sorting looks wrong.
items.checks: Compare query strings with searchSchema: available accepts only true/false, page is zero-based and size is 1–50. Inspect numeric casts and deterministic id sorting in CatalogService.
items.repair: Correct the caller’s query and use the explicit boolean transform and numeric SQL cast. Keep bounds and unknown-key rejection.
items.recovery: available=false&size=2 returns 200 with at most two matching items; available=yes stays 400. Rates sort numerically and equal rates have stable id ordering.

items.title: All database-backed requests slow down: what do you measure first?
items.answer: Pool exhaustion can be a symptom of long work, leaked clients or locks. More connections are not an automatic repair.
items.symptom: Requests queue or fail near the five-second connection-acquisition limit.
items.checks: Inspect pool totalCount, idleCount and waitingCount in an isolated diagnostic; inspect pg_stat_activity and pg_locks for long transactions and blocked queries. Check finally release paths and the catalog lookup held inside inquiry transactions.
items.repair: Fix leaked-client paths or slow/blocking work, bound dependency waits and tune capacity to database limits. Do not terminate sessions or increase max blindly.
items.recovery: Under the same bounded test load, waitingCount returns to zero after completion, transaction age falls, and repeated successful and failed requests do not steadily consume connections.

items.title: Startup reports a changed migration checksum: what is safe?
items.answer: The refusal protects reproducibility; deleting the recorded checksum hides drift rather than repairing it.

source.symbol: changed after application; create a new migration

items.symptom: A service fails startup because an already applied migration changed.
items.checks: Compare the deployed migration version/checksum with the intended source and review the edited SQL. Verify which service-owned database and environment are selected.
items.repair: Restore the original applied file and express the change in a new numbered migration. Rehearse against an isolated database and retain a backup/recovery path.
items.recovery: Old checksums still match, the new migration appears once, a second startup applies nothing, and service acceptance confirms compatible reads/writes.

items.title: An inquiry response timed out: should you submit again?
items.answer: A lost response does not reveal whether the write committed. Preserve its original identity while investigating.

source.symbol: Idempotency key already used for a different inquiry

items.symptom: The browser times out after submitting an inquiry and the user is unsure whether it exists.
items.checks: Recover the original client-scoped key and exact validated payload; check the participant inquiry list and the service’s idempotency path. Identify whether failure happened at catalog lookup, SQL commit or response transport.
items.repair: Retry with the same key and payload. If content must change, first reconcile the original result; do not rotate the key automatically after timeout.
items.recovery: Sequential and concurrent identical retries return one inquiry ID and one outbox event; changed content with the original key returns 409; no unrelated actor can retrieve it.

items.title: Inquiry exists but the inbox is empty: how do you isolate the stage?
items.answer: Follow the durable record through publication and consumption instead of treating an empty inbox as proof the inquiry vanished.
items.symptom: The client sees a committed inquiry while its provider sees no notification.
items.checks: In local service-owned databases, inspect the inquiry’s outbox published_at and event identity, publisher retry logs, broker/topic availability and recipient filter. Inspect consumer CRASH error classification and its restart flag, group membership, committed offsets and actual offset/insert progress. A background consumer may have stopped while the outer loop still sleeps; a green serving probe or stale worker flag is insufficient.
items.repair: Repair the failing local broker/configuration or database dependency. Publisher retries can resume its durable outbox work. For a stopped non-restarting consumer, perform a controlled LOCAL notifications-process restart after the cause is fixed, retaining its group ID, committed offsets and event IDs. Do not insert a replacement inquiry, rotate the group or mark an unsent row published.
items.recovery: During a local rehearsal, verify the original outbox row becomes published, consumer offsets and durable inserts advance, the expected recipient receives one inbox row, replay still leaves one row and an unrelated actor sees none. Explicitly record whether restart was manual; these criteria do not prove automatic recovery.

items.title: A consumer repeatedly fails on one record: what happens next?
items.answer: Malformed JSON or a schema failure prevents the handler from completing. KafkaJS may stop on a non-retriable processing error while this application’s outer loop keeps sleeping; automatic reconnect is not guaranteed. A quarantine/dead-letter workflow is absent. Skipping needs an explicit policy and durable evidence.

source.symbol: throw new Error('Event payload missing; offset is not acknowledged');

items.symptom: The consumer logs the same parse/validation error and its partition makes no useful progress.
items.checks: Identify topic, partition, offset and safe event identity; inspect the failure category without publishing private payloads. Read the CRASH restart flag and check actual processing progress and group membership. Distinguish transient database failures from deterministic malformed JSON or schema incompatibility; readiness alone cannot prove progress.
items.repair: Repair transient dependencies or producer/schema compatibility. If the consumer stopped without restart, perform a controlled LOCAL process restart with the same group and offsets only after fixing the cause. The same poison record will fail again unless corrected or handled through a designed durable quarantine/replay policy; do not delete offsets merely to make readiness green.
items.recovery: A local rehearsal must show the original failing record is successfully processed after compatible repair, or durably retained/quarantined by a separately implemented policy; later valid records advance and replay produces no duplicate inbox effect. Record the manual restart. Existing source does not establish quarantine or automatic recovery.
items.worked_example: The current Nest outbox tutorial provides a separate order service with persistent dead-letter records and administrative requeue. In that example, force a handler to fail through its retry limit, inspect the recorded reason, repair the handler and requeue the same message. Verify one resulting business effect. Its package/version and storage setup are an external design example; this marketplace has no such quarantine flow.

items.title: Local TLS connection fails after certificate changes: what stays enabled?
items.answer: Keep peer verification while checking certificate trust, hostname, expiry and configuration; an encrypted connection to an unverified peer is insufficient.
items.symptom: A database or Kafka client fails with certificate, hostname or authentication errors.
items.checks: Inspect the configured host, certificate authority chain and expiry, clock, TLS flag and environment scope. For pg, check that URL ssl parameters do not replace the explicit CA object. For Kafka, distinguish broker reachability from SCRAM credentials.
items.repair: Restore the correct CA/hostname/credential configuration for the selected environment. Retain rejectUnauthorized true and fix the trust chain instead of disabling checks.
items.recovery: The intended peer connects with verification enabled; a wrong CA or hostname still fails. Re-run a real local query or message round trip, not only a TCP connection probe.

items.title: Login rate limiting changes behind a proxy or replica: why?
items.answer: Process-local state and proxy address interpretation affect the observed rate limit. A public fix needs tests for both abuse resistance and legitimate users.
items.symptom: Many users share a 429 limit, or adding replicas allows more attempts than expected.
items.checks: Inspect request.ip and trusted proxy configuration using synthetic traffic; compare counts per process and the one-minute expiry. Check whether load balancing distributes attempts across independent Maps.
items.repair: Configure only the actual trusted proxy hops and adopt a bounded shared counter if a global limit is required. Do not trust arbitrary forwarded headers or remove throttling.
items.recovery: Synthetic users receive the intended independent limits; spoofed forwarding headers cannot bypass them; repeated attempts across replicas follow the documented policy and expire as expected.

items.title: Which Node version should I install for this project?
items.answer: Start with `node --version` and the package engines, rather than installing whichever version is newest. This backend declares `>=22 <25`; its Dockerfile pins a Node 22 image by digest. Use a patched, supported release inside that range and rerun checks when upgrading. Long-term support (LTS) describes maintenance policy, not proof that every dependency supports that version.

items.title: What do package.json, a lockfile and npm ci each do?
items.answer: `package.json` declares scripts and version ranges; `package-lock.json` records the resolved dependency tree. `npm ci` installs from that agreement and fails on a manifest/lock mismatch instead of updating the lock. Root, backend and frontend are separate package scopes here: run `npm ci`, `npm --prefix backend ci`, and `npm --prefix frontend ci` from the repository root when all tools are needed.

items.title: What must configuration validation establish before listening?
items.answer: Reject missing or malformed settings at startup so requests never reach a half-configured service. `validateConfig` checks the service name, database settings, shared signing secret and capability-specific dependencies. Inquiries also requires a catalog URL. Check variable names and validation messages without printing `.env` or connection strings. Configuration being syntactically valid still does not prove a remote dependency is reachable.

items.answer: `tsc` checks types and emits JavaScript; `node dist/main.js` executes that output. This project uses strict TypeScript and ECMAScript modules (ESM), with NodeNext resolution. The container copies migrations, seeds and certificates as runtime assets too. items.title: What is shared when four services use the same Docker image?
items.answer: They share packaged code and dependencies, not one JavaScript heap or domain database. Each container selects one capability with `SERVICE` and receives its own database login. A shared PostgreSQL server or broker remains a shared failure risk. Container memory and CPU limits constrain resources; they do not make workloads highly available.

items.title: What does a mock prove compared with a real integration test?
items.answer: A mock supplies controlled dependency behavior; a spy records calls. A Jest test can prove that a denial branch avoids an insert against a fake database. It cannot prove PostgreSQL actually blocks a concurrent write or Kafka recovers after restart. Pair those tests with real dependency scenarios for durability, locking and replay. Choose tests by the failure they could catch.

items.title: How do I test a race without hoping it happens?
items.answer: Control the schedule. In the stale-search test, keep the first promise unresolved, issue another search, resolve the newer response, then resolve the older response last. Assert the latest results stay visible. Vitest runs that hook test; a simulated browser document is useful for state behavior but does not reproduce real browser layout. Avoid arbitrary sleeps when explicit promise control can reproduce the failure.

items.title: What do type checking, linting, unit tests, build and acceptance each establish?
items.answer: Type checking rejects inconsistent static types; linting checks source rules; unit tests exercise selected behavior; a build proves artifacts can be emitted. Acceptance sends real application programming interface (API) requests through nginx to services and dependencies. None substitutes for the others. Run the root check/test/build scripts, then local acceptance against port 8180 when the stack is running; inspect failed cases rather than changing expected results to force green.

items.title: Why keep a real browser test after API tests pass?
items.answer: An API response does not prove that a person can open a modal, use a keyboard or recover from an error. The browser smoke uses Playwright against the actual site; component tests provide faster focused feedback. Browser checks and screenshots cover selected journeys, not complete accessibility or all supported browsers. Record the tested URL, source revision and actual assertions.

items.title: Why does fetch need both catch and a response-status check?
items.answer: A fetch promise may fulfill for a server error such as 404 or 500; those are HTTP responses, not network failures. Check `res.ok` and translate error bodies safely. This API helper separately handles 204 so it does not parse an empty body as JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). A TypeScript return type cannot validate a server’s JSON at runtime.

items.title: Why use abort plus a stale-response guard?
items.answer: When a search changes, abort the old request and prevent old continuations from updating current state. The hook checks the aborted signal before applying results, errors and loading state. Cleanup also aborts on unmount. Cancellation reduces wasted work; it does not reverse a server transaction that already committed. Retry uncertain writes with the original idempotency identity.

items.title: Which state belongs in React and which belongs in the backend?
items.answer: Props pass data to a component; state triggers renders; a ref holds mutable coordination without triggering a render. Context shares authentication and hooks reuse effects; route components compose pages while services call APIs. Browser storage here remembers a token, comparison IDs and uncertain-write intent. Committed profiles, inquiries and notifications remain authoritative in service-owned databases; browser storage cannot replace them.

items.title: Why preserve the original inquiry key after a network failure?
items.answer: A network failure may hide a successful commit. This hook saves the key and canonical payload in session storage before sending. Reuse that pair to reconcile or retry; a new key could create a second inquiry. The saved attempt is intent, not evidence of a committed record. A successful API response or durable read establishes the business result.

items.title: How do I explain a CI workflow without claiming deployment happened?
items.answer: Continuous integration (CI) runs configured jobs on specific source. Here source, integration and Terraform jobs provide different evidence; deployment is separate. A workflow file describes intended execution, while an actual run and its artifacts establish results. Job dependencies determine ordering; steps inside a job run sequentially. Quote the observed run and commit before describing an external integration as verified.

items.title: What does a Sonar quality gate add, and what are its limits?
items.answer: A quality gate applies configured conditions to submitted analysis, including the chosen coverage scope. Editor feedback is a different stage. The local Sonar helper waits for a real gate result; its existence is not a successful hosted scan. Review exclusions and missing reports. A passing gate still needs meaningful authorization and failure-path tests; no measured generated-code percentage follows from it.

items.title: How should I review a dependency update or security advisory?
items.answer: Inspect direct and transitive changes, the advisory’s affected path and the runtime/build distinction. This project audits production dependencies and has scoped overrides; an override needs compatibility tests and an exit condition. Dependabot proposes changes rather than approving them. Keep the lockfile consistent; an audit result is a dated advisory check, not proof that application authorization is safe.

items.title: How are short-lived release identity and application identity different?
items.answer: OpenID Connect (OIDC) lets a CI job exchange an identity token for scoped cloud credentials after configured trust checks. That workload identity is separate from a user’s JSON Web Token (JWT) used by the marketplace. Bind release evidence to the exact source commit and image digest; a movable image tag alone cannot identify the bytes deployed. This lesson explains configured controls, not a new cloud release.

items.answer: Write the expected behavior and negative cases, inspect the actual diff, update its requirement/specification and traceability, then run tests that could reject the change. items.title: How would cache-aside preserve correct provider results?
items.answer: Cache-aside checks a cache, reads the authoritative store on a miss, then caches the result. Include every response-changing input and tenant/authorization scope in keys. Choose a time to live (TTL) and invalidation rule, and avoid many simultaneous misses overwhelming PostgreSQL (a cache stampede). A cache hit can still be stale. This application has no shared cache; PostgreSQL remains authoritative. Negative caching briefly remembers a not-found result; it needs its own expiry and must not leak authorization decisions. Coordinate concurrent misses and add expiry jitter so many keys do not refill together.

items.title: How would I model a DynamoDB query instead of replacing SQL with Scan?
items.answer: Start from access patterns. To list a user’s notifications, a partition key selects the user and a sort key orders their records. Query requires one partition-key value; Scan examines a broader scope and is not a substitute for a missing access pattern. Secondary indexes add costs and read-consistency choices. No DynamoDB table exists here; a migration needs explicit backfill and ownership design. Denormalization stores access-pattern-specific copies instead of joining them at read time. Define how edits update those copies and how backfill catches up with concurrent writes before cutover.

items.title: Do many partition keys and TTL guarantee safe DynamoDB writes?
items.answer: No. One busy key can dominate traffic even with many distinct keys. A conditional create can reject a repeated event identity; a transaction coordinates a defined set of operations. items.title: How do a queue, pub/sub, an event bus and a workflow differ?
items.answer: A work queue distributes tasks; publish/subscribe (pub/sub) gives independent subscribers their own event paths; an event bus routes by rules; a workflow tracks steps and failure transitions. Kafka currently retains a partitioned log for replay. In Simple Queue Service (SQS), processing normally ends by deleting the message. A visibility timeout can expire after a committed effect, so retries still need durable idempotency and a monitored dead-letter queue (DLQ).

items.title: What do FIFO groups and partial batch failure actually guarantee?
items.answer: First-in-first-out (FIFO) ordering is scoped to a message group; one busy group limits parallelism. Broker deduplication has a finite window and cannot make database effects exactly once. A Lambda SQS batch can repeat successful items when one fails. With ReportBatchItemFailures configured, report failed item IDs; for FIFO stop after failure and report unprocessed items too to preserve order.

items.title: How would an event-triggered Lambda differ from this listening Nest process?
items.answer: An event handler receives an invocation payload and returns or throws; this Nest app creates a server and listens on a port. Validate the specific trigger’s event/response contract, initialize reusable clients outside repeated handler work and await required effects. Authentication, gateway invocation permission and business authorization are separate checks. An API Gateway design must choose required HTTP API or REST API features deliberately; no such resources exist here.

items.title: Why must Lambda retry and concurrency policy depend on its trigger?
items.answer: A synchronous caller observes a failure and decides its retry policy; asynchronous invocation and polled queues have different retry mechanisms. More concurrent handlers can multiply downstream database connections, so cap concurrency and connection use against the database budget. Cold initialization adds work before an invocation. Do not assume one universal retry count, an always-warm process, or that Promise.all makes downstream capacity unlimited.

items.title: What would useful tracing show across the inquiry and notification flow?
items.answer: A trace links spans describing work across boundaries. Instrument the request, catalog lookup and transaction, then propagate context or links through the later outbox publish and Kafka consume. A trace ID is not a durable idempotency key. Bound attribute values and avoid secrets; sampling or exporter drops can hide work. There is no installed OpenTelemetry pipeline here, so shared log fields do not establish distributed tracing.

items.title: How do SLI, SLO and an error budget guide an incident?
items.answer: A service-level indicator (SLI) measures a user outcome; a service-level objective (SLO) sets its target over a window. The error budget is the permitted unsuccessful fraction. A 99% target over 1,000 eligible requests permits ten failures. Measure accepted inquiries separately from notification delay. A health response is not that business measure. Investigate hypotheses using latency, errors, backlog and dependency saturation; record impact and recovery in a post-incident note. A service-level agreement (SLA) is an external commitment with consequences; an internal SLO is not automatically an SLA. Burn rate compares observed failures with the budget’s permitted rate over the same basis.
items.worked_example: Use the official example SLO document structure: name the journey, eligible denominator, success rule, observation window and owner. For 1,000 eligible inquiries and 15 failures, the 99% target is missed by five. This is synthetic arithmetic, not a measured production SLO.

items.title: How would a saga recover when several services cannot share one transaction?
items.answer: Keep each local transaction inside its owning service. A saga coordinates steps and compensating business actions when later steps fail; compensation is not automatically a database rollback. Retry only a bounded, repeat-safe operation and preserve its stable identity. Step Functions can express retry and catch transitions, but repeated task effects still need idempotency. This project implements an outbox flow, not a saga engine.
items.worked_example: Read the official Retry/Catch state examples. Inspect the predicted execution states rather than treating retries as an atomic transaction.
