items.title: What proves recovery after database failover or restoration?
items.answer: A reconnected socket is only one layer. Re-establish connections with bounded retries, verify migrations and ownership, read expected rows and test a new write/event journey. A recovery point objective (RPO) limits data loss; a recovery time objective (RTO) limits time to recovery. Measure both with recorded timestamps and known records. Read replicas serve reads and are not an automatic writer failover or tested backup. Cold recovery rebuilds from retained data; warm recovery keeps some capacity ready; hot recovery keeps live capacity. Their costs and recovery times need a tested design, not a label.

items.title: What changes when a Node service scales to more process replicas?
items.answer: Each process has its own heap, connection pool and in-memory throttle. More replicas can increase database connections or broker consumers without fixing the bottleneck. Keep durable data outside process memory, measure latency/errors/saturation and allow for startup delay. Rolling and blue-green releases both need schema compatibility; a healthy new process alone does not establish business acceptance. Rolling replacement mixes old and new replicas during rollout; blue-green keeps two environments and switches traffic. These deployment alternatives are design extensions, not activated release strategies in this guide.

items.title: Why is secret rotation a state transition instead of a text edit?
items.answer: A secret is credential data; an encryption key controls cryptographic operations. Rotation must update the credential authority and clients coherently, including old/new overlap and recovery if only one side changes. Never put values in source, logs or infrastructure-state exports. These processes read settings at startup; editing a secret store does not hot-refresh their pools or signing keys. Automatic application rotation is absent. Encryption-key rotation is different from password rotation: older key material may still be needed to decrypt retained data. A disabled or deleted decryption key can make a backup unusable; restoration therefore depends on usable keys as well as data.

items.title: How do logs, metrics, traces and administrative audit differ?
items.answer: Logs describe individual events, metrics summarize measurements, traces relate work across boundaries, and administrative audit records identity/action/outcome for management operations. Correlate them by time and appropriate IDs, but a cloud audit event does not prove an inquiry was persisted. Keep metric labels bounded (service/status rather than every user ID), protect retention/access and verify collection plus export instead of assuming console output reached a backend. Management events describe control-plane operations; data events describe operations such as S3 object reads. Default administrative event history is not complete data-access audit and does not record this app’s SQL business actions.

items.title: What would prove that a monitoring alarm works?
items.answer: A metric alarm evaluates measurements over configured periods; missing data policy and the threshold affect its state. A resource declaration proves configuration, not signal arrival or responder delivery. Define an actionable user symptom, a query that narrows the failing layer and a controlled exercise with timestamps. This guide performs no new cloud alarm or delivery test.

This backend configures ts-jest for ECMAScript modules (ESM), treats TypeScript test files as ESM and maps relative .js imports back to source. Jest also uses Node’s experimental VM-module support here. A transformer emits executable code; it does not prove runtime input validity. Check package type, transform settings and source specifiers together before changing imports to satisfy one tool.

items.title: Where do the demo users come from, and is that a sign-up API?

Catalog separately seeds provider profiles. This is controlled laboratory initialization, not public registration or shared identity tables. An existing database volume retains prior records. items.repair: Abort obsolete reads and guard every state continuation. Reconcile/retry the uncertain inquiry with its existing identity rather than creating a new attempt.
items.recovery: The stale-response regression keeps current results; retrying the same inquiry returns one durable inquiry and eventually one notification effect.

items.title: Tests pass but the API route fails through nginx
items.answer: Check the complete routed path instead of treating unit success as deployment proof.
items.symptom: A unit suite passes, but a browser request returns 404, 502 or an HTML body.
items.checks: Record the exact method/path/status/content type. Check frontend proxy routing, target service readiness and matching source/image. A direct API port bypasses nginx and is a different path.
items.repair: Repair the incorrect route, proxy target or unhealthy dependency at its owning layer. Preserve contract paths and management-route isolation.
items.recovery: Replay the same request through http://localhost:8180, including a negative authorization case, then run the real acceptance suite and inspect its individual results.

items.symptom: An older app starts, but deleted records or incompatible schema still break a journey.
items.checks: Record source/image/schema versions, the destructive change and last usable backup point. Check whether the old app can read the current schema before changing traffic.
items.repair: Choose a compatible forward repair or rehearsed restore to an isolated target. Verify data and credentials before a controlled cutover; do not overwrite the only recoverable copy.
items.recovery: Check known rows and timestamps, new write/read/event behavior, ownership denials and measured data-loss/recovery intervals against RPO/RTO; image health alone is insufficient.

items.title: After scaling, database saturation increases while request latency worsens
items.answer: Scaling a process can amplify a constrained dependency.
items.symptom: More application replicas coincide with pool waits, connection errors or higher latency.
items.checks: Count processes and per-process pool limits; measure active/waiting clients, query duration, database capacity and traffic. Separate CPU pressure from connection/query bottlenecks.
items.repair: Bound concurrency and reduce amplification; repair slow queries or leaked clients before adding replicas. Size the total connection budget for all capabilities and administrative headroom.
items.recovery: Under the same bounded local test load, waiting clients and errors stabilize, latency improves and real write/read/event checks still pass. No new cloud scaling is executed.
